Explain how the program is consistent with the published role and mission of the institution and how it is related to the institution’s academic planning.
Embracing Rhode Island ’s heritage of independent thought, we value: As stated in the URI’s mission statement, our institutional values: o Creativity and scholarship o Diversity, fairness, and respect o Engaged learning and civic involvement o Intellectual and ethical leadership The program that we are proposing is not only consistent with those key guiding principles, but it can have a significant impact by strengthening those values in our learning community and RI society.

Our program, based on rigorous scholarship, will help to shape the face of education in the state.
The RI Department of Education is about to approve new high school graduation requirements that include the study of the same World Language for two years.
A new WL Education Program could potentially attract more heritage speakers into the teaching profession.
This will increase the diversity among faculty in our schools and will provide multilingual students with role models with whom they can identify.
We anticipate that our graduates will become

5 leaders and advocates in multicultural and multilingual education: from a very early stage we will foster collaboration with regional associations such as the RI Foreign Language Association (RIFLA) or the Coalition for a Multilingual RI.
As a matter of fact, I currently serve as university liaison for RIFLA and Sarah Steverman (current RIFLA President) has been a guest presenter in my EDC 485 (Seminar of teaching) class.
The new proposed program of study will help our graduates develop their intercultural skills and acquire a “glocal” perspective, that is, the capacity to understand how local and global events are interconnected and the effects that they have on each other.

Estimate the projected impact of this program on other public higher education institutions in Rhode Island (e.g. loss of students or revenues), provide a rationale for the assumptions made in the projections, and indicate the manner in which the other public institutions were consulted in developing the projections.
Have you communicated with other institutions about the development of this program and have any concerns been raised related to role, scope, and mission or duplication.
Our program will not create any new competition to attract students that will be detrimental for other RI institutions of higher education, as the intent of the program is to adjust an already existing academic offering to the new certification reality implemented by the RI Department of Education.
The impact of the program will not be noticeable to other WL Education Programs around the state, only to the URI students that would benefit from a curriculum that better adjusts to their future professional needs.

To the best of my knowledge there are four other higher ed institutions in RI that offer World Language Education programs: Salve Regina, Rhode Island College, Providence College and Roger Williams University.
None of these programs is new: such programs have been in place for at least 10 years.
In all those cases, the original World Language programs were part of the Secondary Education programs, just one of the multiple tracks that students could take.
Two of those institutions have already taken steps to adapt to the new RIDE certification reality.
Recently, in both Salve Regina and RIC the World Language Program has become independent.
According to the information listed on their websites, the World Language Education program is still a track of the Secondary Education Program in the cases of both Providence College (<https://academics.providence.edu/secondary-education/>) and Roger Williams University (<https://www.rwu.edu/undergraduate/academics/programs/secondary-education>).

The new URI World Language Education program will fill a void that currently exists in the world language teacher preparation programs by focusing on providing more comprehensive preparation to our candidates so they can be effective teachers at the elementary and secondary levels, and it will allow us to continue being the leader in preparing future world language educators in the state of RI.

The graduation requirements will be comparable to the ones at the other RI institutions of higher education that offer programs in World Language Education: Institution Total credits EDC credits Language credits URI 120 42 30 Salve 120 34 37 RIC 120 48 48-40 PC 120 42 30 RWU 120 31 30 As previously mentioned, upon completion of our program and after successfully completing the licensure tests, our well-prepared graduates will be ready to apply for the Rhode Island World Language teacher certification in grades K-12.

The RIDE certification requirements for World Language teachers are:4 ● Bachelor’s degree from a regionally accredited institution ● Completion of an approved program or Credential Review Consortium Institution (CRCI) credential review plan for the preparation of All Grades World Language Teachers in a specific language ● Completion of a minimum of 12 weeks of student teaching in this area and a minimum of 60 hours field experience prior to student teaching ● Demonstration of meeting the pedagogical competencies of the Rhode Island Professional Teaching Standards (RIPTS) ● Demonstration of meeting the content competencies as prescribed by the American Council for the Teaching of Foreign Languages (ACTFL) Other requirements: ● Meet all Rhode Island pedagogy and subject matter testing requirements for this certificate area 4 See: <https://www.ride.ri.gov/Portals/0/Uploads/Documents/Teachers-and-Administrators-Excellent- Educators/Educator-Certification/Cert-Requirements/tbd_AG-World%20Languages-Req.pdf?ver=2015-01-22- 123036-823>.
The RIDE has stated that taking the PRAXIS II exam will not be a certification requirement in the near future.

12 Assessment Requirements: All applicants must meet the following Rhode Island assessment requirements: ● Applicants must achieve a passing score of 160 on the Praxis II Principals of Learning and Teaching – Grades K-6 Test (5622) OR a passing score of 157 on the Praxis II Principals of Learning and Teaching – Grades 7-12 test (5624) AND a passing score of 162 on the French World Language Test (5174), a passing score of 163 on the German World Language Test (5183), a passing score of 161 on the Latin Test (5601), a passing score of 168 on the Spanish World Language Test (5195), or a passing score of Advanced Low on all other world languages – Oral Proficiency Interview. ● Applicants prepared in a program where the language of instruction was not English must achieve a passing core of 64 on the Versant Pro Speaking and Writing English assessments.

We are currently trying to attract more heritage speakers of world languages into the teaching profession.
We are contacting students that have taken SPA 210: Spanish for Heritage Speakers and sharing information with them about the different career paths and employment opportunities that they will have upon graduation if they complete our program.
We are also underlining to them that they could have a direct and significant impact on their communities.
As mentioned above, one of the purposes of the new program is to attract, retain, and graduate more teachers from multicultural, multilingual, historically marginalized, and under-represented groups in the education profession.
The inclusion of coursework in Bilingual Education and Teaching English as a Second Language aims to attract and harness the unique talents and lived experiences of students from our important local and regional multilingual communities.
In addition to this, the RI Department of Education, through the work of the Rhode Island Council on Elementary and Secondary Education, is currently in the process of changing the state’s high school graduation requirements.

Among the proposed changes to the system, students will be required to take a minimum of two years of study of the same language in order to successfully graduate from high school.
This change has the potential to strengthen the general pipeline of

13 candidates for our proposed World Language Education-All Grades program. Finally, given both the regional and national shortage of world language educators, as evidenced by the 100% employment rates of graduates from our existing program and the high percentage of new language teachers who are being hired through an emergency certification process, the demand for well-qualified K-12 world language educators is high and the urgent need for this program is clear. JCAP Pre-Proposal Form Revised 2021 Joint Committee on Academic Planning Pre-Proposal for New Programs Part I: Title and affiliation(s) of proposed program: Program Title: World Language Education Program Degree Type: B.A.
Proposer(s): Iñaki Pérez Ibáñez, Assistant Professor in Spanish and Teacher Education Department(s): School of Education College(s): College of Education and Professional Studies Part II.
Briefly provide the following information (not to exceed two pages): The School of Education currently offers a Bachelor of Arts degree in Secondary Education, with multiple tracks reflecting various specializations.
Since its inception, the World Language Education Program has been one of these tracks (the other tracks are English, History/Social Studies, Mathematics, and Science).
Upon graduation, students in the Secondary Education Program obtain certification to teach at the High School level (grades 7-12).

Upon the completion of an additional course and a teach ing practicum at a Middle School, students in this existing program also have the option to obtain a Middle School extension, a credential that allows them to teach in grades 5-8 in any Rhode Island elementary, middle, or junior high school.
Recently the Rhode Island Department of Education changed the World Language teacher certification system.
Due to these changes, graduates from our current Secondary Education – World Language program are now certified to teach in Rhode Island at all levels of elementary, middle, and secondary education (grades PK-12).
The new program proposal is intended address the changes in Rhode Island certification regulations, which will require significant changes (over 25%) to the requirements for our current BA in Secondary Education with a specialization in World Languages, effectively transforming it into a BA in World Language Education -All Grades.

In the proposed new program, students will take a variety of existing EDC courses in Elementary Education, Early Childhood Education, Secondary Education, and Teaching English as a Second Language / Bilingual Education concentrations so that, upon graduation, they will be more versatile and highly employable educators who are better prepared to teach effectively in a wider variety of educational settings.
The financial cost to the university of this new program will be zero, as our students will be required to take existing courses that are regularly offered in the School o f Education.
The development of new courses will not be necessary to implement the proposed overhaul of the program.
The new program will not require the hiring of any new faculty (neither full time nor adjunct faculty).

JCAP Pre-Proposal Form Revised 2021 One of the purposes of the new program is to attract, retain, and graduate more teachers from multicultural, multilingual, historically marginalized, and under-represented groups in the education profession.
The inclusion of coursework in Bilingual Education and Teaching English as a Second Language aims to attract and harness the unique talents and lived experiences of students from our important local and regional multilingual communities.
In addition to this, the RI Department of Education, through the work of the Rhode Island Council on Elementary and Secondary Education, is currently in the process of changing the state’s high school graduation requirements.
Among the proposed changes to the system, students will be required to take a minimum of two years of study of the same language in order to successfully graduate from high school.
This change has the potential to strengthen the general pipeline of candidates for our proposed World Langua ge Education-All Grades program.

Finally, given both the regional and national shortage of world language educators, as evidenced by the 100% employment rates of graduates from our existing program and the high percentage of new language teachers who are being hired through an emergency certification process, the demand for well-qualified K-12 world language educators is high and the urgent need for this program is clear.

CASC Procedures

The Curriculum and Standards Committee (CASC) Procedures CASC examines course and program proposals to ensure they are comprehensible and user-friendly for undergraduate students.
Within the Kuali proposal, we examine all ﬁelds to conﬁrm clear details vital to student success, such as prerequisites, course rationale and description, the number of seats and sections offered per year, and syllabi.
Syllabi should accompany all major course proposals (new classes, signiﬁcant modiﬁcations to a course).
To ensure proposal syllabi will be clear to students, we look for: ● straight-forward course information (class description & objectives, method of instruction); ● clear course policies, structures, and methods of teaching; ● clarity regarding grade scale & methods, assignments, and how coursework connects to credit hours; ● current information about accessible technological resources and apps necessary for the class; Further, students are best served by having up-to-date information on support services such as DAI; illness policies; and procedures reﬂecting current University standards.
Where these items are overlooked or out-of-date, CASC may provide friendly feedback.

Also, ATL has resources and templates for syllabi ( https://web.uri.edu/atl/design/syllabus/ ).
New courses should provide supporting documentation uploaded by the chair of the department/academic unit into the proper Kuali ﬁeld, indicating the date that their department/program voted to approve the course.
Program-level proposals should include all materials relevant to the new program/proposed changes, including supporting documentation from other academic units impacted by these changes.
All program and applicable accreditation requirements should be listed .
The Kuali ﬁelds for program proposals should include courses impacted by changes.
Course and Program Overlap Overlap is when a newly proposed or modiﬁed course/program intersects with the content of an existing course or program.
The amount of overlap might range from small (the topics of a single class) to approaching virtual duplication.
Proposers and curriculum approval committees can use search features within Kuali to compare other current and proposed courses/programs for potential overlap.

When CASC recognizes potential overlap, they will ask the course proposer and department/instructor to consult regarding the degree and signiﬁcance of overlap.
Even with substantial replication in content, there might be key differences in approach.
As CASC cannot be experts in all disciplines, we request that the proposer and faculty for the existing course/program work together.
This collaboration can be documented in a statement communicating the resolution to CASC.
If this collaboration cannot occur, CASC exercises its best judgment regarding student beneﬁt.
Note: overlap issues can also be addressed on the Faculty Senate ﬂoor or even at ﬁnal approval with the President.
We also encourage colleges to check for overlap themselves.
Starting in Fall 2025, CASC’s ‘Proposed Temporary and Permanent Courses/Programs’ email will be distributed at the end of the last full week of each month.
We encourage each college’s curriculum committee to meet during the ﬁrst full week of each month and, as part of their deliberations, carefully consider all newly proposed offerings in that CASC newsletter for potential overlap.

Any overlapping courses/programs should be reported to Genviéve Spitale ( genvieve.spitale@uri.edu ); the course/program will not be reviewed until the originating and overlapping colleges agree in writing that either the original proposal or a revised version can move forward for CASC/Gen Ed/Grad Council consideration.

5.10.10 Committees, Boards, Councils and other such entities which have a university-wide function are described in this chapter. With few exceptions, committees with a narrower scope are not included here. For information on them, consult policy documents of various campus units, such as college by-laws, where available, and the Graduate Student Manual. Standing committees of the Faculty Senate, although having university-wide function, can be found in the by-laws of the Faculty Senate.

5.10.11 The committees included here are organized according to the jurisdictional rubric under which they fall, and are divided into (1) committees falling under presidential jurisdiction; (2) committees falling under direct jurisdiction of the general faculty or of the Graduate Faculty; and (3) committees falling under the joint purview of the Faculty Senate and the President. The division into the various jurisdictional rubrics has been proposed by a Faculty Senate Constitution, By-Laws, and University Manual (CBUM) subcommittee on the basis of research conducted during the 2001-02 academic year. This research primarily took into consideration the jurisdictional divide between the President (administration) and the Faculty Senate resulting from Article II of the Senate Constitution; when this was not conclusive, the historic understanding of who had jurisdiction at the time of the establishment of a committee or its predecessor was taken into account. In most cases, these criteria allowed a clear determination of a committee’s jurisdictional rubric. To limit future disputes about jurisdiction, the subcommittee proposed that the Faculty Senate endorse and accept the jurisdictional division resulting from the subcommittee’s research, the senate did so at its meeting on November 11, 2003, and the President endorsed the senate legislation on December 5, 2003.

5.10.12 Faculty, administrators, and staff members are expected to serve on committees, if designated. Each standing committee of the University shall make an annual report for the academic year to its appointing authority.

5.25.10 The Institutional Review Board (IRB) shall review and approve all biomedical and behavioral research involving human subjects which is conducted or sponsored by the University. The Code of Federal Regulations, 45 CFR 46, revised in 2005, requires the existence of this committee in order to protect the rights and welfare of the human subjects of such research. See Appendix G for the University’s policy and procedures concerning the protection of human subjects.

5.25.11 The IRB shall comprise at least five members appointed by the President. The chairperson shall be recommended by the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs to the President, to be appointed for one three-year term. Other IRB members shall be appointed for two-year, renewable terms. The IRB shall not consist entirely of men, entirely of women, or entirely of members of one profession. At least one member shall be a person whose primary training and research concerns are in nonscientific areas; for example, lawyers or members of the clergy. At least one member shall be a person who is not otherwise affiliated with the institution or part of the immediate family of a person who is affiliated with the institution. One member shall be a person whose primary training and research concerns are in the scientific area, for example a physician, a biologist, or a psychologist. When research is reviewed involving a category of vulnerable subjects (e.g., prisoners, children, individuals institutionalized as mentally disabled), the IRB shall include at least one member who has as a primary concern the welfare of these subjects. The Vice President for Research and Economic Development or the Vice President’s designee shall serve ex officio , as a non-voting member. An effort will be made to appoint members so that the IRB will be sufficiently qualified through the experience and expertise of its members, the diversity of their racial and cultural backgrounds, and their sensitivity to community attitudes, to be respected for its advice and counsel in safeguarding the rights and welfare of human subjects.

5.25.12 To avoid conflict of interest, an IRB member shall not participate in the IRB’s review of any project in which the member is involved as a researcher or subject.

The Diving Control Board also serves as a search committee for the Diving Safety Officer and provides advice and counsel to the Vice President for Research and Economic Development who makes the appointment.

NEW CERTIFICATES, MINORS, or SPECIALIZATIONS COLLEGE OF EDUCATION: Minor in Global Education Studies, see Appendix H Global Education Studies (GES) minor allows students to explore globalization and internationalization of education and educational policies using the critical lens of equity and social justice, human rights and global citizenship.
The minor will prepare students with a diversity of backgrounds with the skill sets to become change agents and leaders in education in today’s globalized world.
This minor is part of the College of Education, as K-16 education are important components of the program.
However, students from all majors are welcome to participate or take courses in the minor.
Students interested in pursuing careers in and outside of the U.S. in the field of K-16 education, governmental and non-governmental organizations, international agencies, further their studies of international issues are especially encouraged to pursue this minor.
The curriculum is focused on expanding students’ knowledge, skills, and understanding of specific comparative and international theories, concepts, and practices in education.

The minor includes a requirement for participation in a faculty-led program in one of the College of Education’s study abroad programs in education or equivalent international experience such as COIL.
To declare a minor in Global Studies in Education a student must contact their major academic advisor at their College.
A program advisor at the College of Education will facilitate the students’ progress toward the minor and help assure that all requirements will be met for completion of the minor.
Minor Requirements: Global Education Studies (GES) minors must complete 18 or more credits related to global, comparative, and international education offered by different departments.
Requirements include a core of nine credits at the College of Education as follows: 1) EDC441-Comparative and International Education; 2) EDC330-Introduction to MLL Education; 3) Participation in a Faculty led study abroad program or an internship that is equivalent (i.e.
COIL (Collaborative Online International Learning, transfer course from another study abroad program).
We have a partnership with BridgeTEFL, students can transfer credits from this program, toward certification to teach English abroad.

Students will also choose a minimum of one language course from the Languages department or proficiency in another language that may not be offered in the languages department.
This can be waived for a student who has grown up in a multilingual household, or who has lived and studied at least three years or more in a foreign country including grades 1-12 (or equivalent).
For those students, these three credits can be replaced with electives.
Finally, students will take two electives from the approved courses.
Non-Education majors must also take EDC103 G in place of one of their electives.
Other international/global courses may be used as electives if approved by advisor.
